title: From the Rubble of University to Building a New Future
paragraphs: For me, the war was never news I heard from a distance.
It became part of the fabric of my daily life — it touched my studies, my family, and the dreams I once thought were following a clear path.
I saw how destruction could change a person's life in an instant, how places built for learning could be abandoned or damaged, and how access to education itself could become a struggle.
And yet, I kept my belief that education is something we must never lose.
When the traditional path became harder, I looked for another one, and I found in distance learning a chance to keep going.
I studied from home, learned to take responsibility for my own time and future, and kept studying despite the circumstances around me.
The degree was never just a personal achievement to me.
I saw it as proof that destruction may stop at buildings, but it must never reach a person's will.
Today, as I look toward Syria's future, I don't want to remain a prisoner of what happened.
I want to be part of the next chapter.
I want to use what I've learned to help rebuild our institutions and to help the next generation reach a better education.
message: We tell our stories because we want to learn from the past, not stay trapped in it.
We don't want to use Syrians' suffering against the state or society.
We want to use it to build a stronger state, educational institutions better able to embrace their children, and a system that lets every graduate put their knowledge in service of their country.
Schools and universities can be rebuilt — but building the person is the most important task of all.
excerpt: We tell our stories because we want to learn from the past, not stay trapped in it.

title: The War Didn't Only Destroy Buildings — It Cut Off Many Roads to the Future
paragraphs: I grew up at a time when education felt like something natural to us.
We went to school, then thought about university, work, and the future.
But the war made a great many of these things uncertain.
Areas were damaged, ways of life changed, and many students were forced to relocate, stop, or search for alternatives.
I was one of those forced to change my educational plan.
But I didn't want to let circumstances have the final word.
I began a new journey in distance education, knowing full well the road wouldn't be easy.
I studied under conditions that were far from ideal, facing the challenges of internet access, electricity, the pressures of daily life, and family responsibilities.
But every subject I completed felt like a step toward reclaiming something I felt the war had taken from me: the sense that I had a future I could build for myself.
I graduated — but I never saw the certificate as the end of the journey.
On the contrary, I began thinking more about a bigger question:
How can our generation contribute to rebuilding the country?
We need engineers, doctors, teachers, administrators, technicians, researchers — every person with knowledge and skill.
That's why recognizing graduates and enabling them to work and continue their education isn't just an individual issue.
It's part of investing in Syria's future.
message: We don't want to use the years of war to condemn our present.
We want to use the lessons those years left us to build a better future.
What was destroyed can be rebuilt, what was cut off can be reconnected, and the educated person is the first stone in that process of rebuilding.
excerpt: We don't want to use the years of war to condemn our present.

title: From Years of Displacement to the Dream of Returning and Contributing
paragraphs: During the years of war, the meaning of the word "home" changed for me.
Place stopped being something fixed, and life became full of movement and uncertainty.
But the one thing I tried to hold on to, no matter what else changed, was my education.
I believed that if I had lost so much already, I shouldn't lose my future too.
So I kept learning whenever I could, and I benefited from distance education when access to a traditional university became difficult.

I studied amid the responsibilities of daily life, and sometimes amid difficult psychological and financial circumstances, but I always told myself that the knowledge I gained today might one day become part of the solution my country needs.
I made it to graduation.
But afterward I realized how many other graduates were facing similar challenges moving from a degree to work or further study.
That's when I began to see the issue differently.
It was no longer only about my own future.
It was about the future of an entire generation that could play a real role in rebuilding Syria.
message: We don't want the stories of war to be a source of division.
We want them to be a way to understand what people need today.
We don't want to use the destruction against the state; we want to help build the state after years of destruction.
And we want the Syrian graduate to be part of this rebuilding — not someone left standing outside it because of an obstacle that can be resolved.
excerpt: We don't want the stories of war to be a source of division.

title: When Everything Stopped… Education Remained a Path to the Future
paragraphs: During the years of war, I watched how crises could bring so much of a person's life to a halt.
Studies stop, work is disrupted, families are scattered, and cities change.
But I learned there is one thing we must never stop building, whatever the circumstances: the human being.
That's why I chose to keep pursuing my education.
It wasn't a traditional path, and the conditions were far from ideal, but I found a way to learn and grow.
I worked alongside my studies, carried different responsibilities, and tried to turn the hard years into experience rather than letting them go to waste.
And when I graduated, I didn't feel like I had reached the end.
I felt like I had taken on a greater responsibility.
If Syria needs to rebuild its schools, universities, and institutions, it needs, above all, its educated sons and daughters.
message: Every Syrian graduate is capable of being part of the solution.
We don't want to keep talking only about the destruction.
We want to talk about rebuilding.
And we don't want our degrees to be a reason to leave the country — we want them to be tools we bring back to our community, contributing to its future.
We must learn from the past, build in the present, and shape the future through education.
excerpt: Every Syrian graduate is capable of being part of the solution.

title: The Journey of Education Was Never an Escape from the Homeland… but an Attempt to Return to It Stronger
paragraphs: I grew up watching the effects of war all around me.
Neighborhoods changed, buildings were damaged, and families were forced to rebuild their lives again and again.
In the middle of all that, one question stayed with me:
How can our generation start again?
I found my answer in education.
I began a distance university degree, knowing I wasn't studying just to earn a certificate.
I wanted to gain knowledge that would one day let me be useful to my country.
The years passed, and I graduated.
When I began thinking about the next stage, I realized there was a need for clear solutions to help graduates make use of their qualifications inside Syria.
That's when I understood that the issue of recognition isn't just a paperwork matter.
It concerns the future of thousands of people who could be part of rebuilding the country.
message: We don't want to see the state as an adversary.
We want the state to be a partner in the solution.

And we don't want to use stories of destruction and suffering to reopen wounds — we want to document them so we can understand the scale of what the Syrian people have lost, and what they need to start again.
Our goal is for the graduate to move from asking about their future to actively taking part in shaping it.
The Syria we want to build needs all its sons and daughters — their knowledge, their experience, and their dreams.
excerpt: We don't want to see the state as an adversary.

title: After Years of Loss… We Want to Be Part of the Recovery
paragraphs: Over the past years, Syrians have lost a great deal.
We lost homes, places of learning, job opportunities, and a stability that once seemed ordinary.
But there's another loss we cannot allow to continue: the loss of the educated person who finds no path to use their knowledge.
That's why I keep calling for solutions that help Syrian graduates move from education into work, study, and contributing to society.
I don't want my story to be a story of complaint.
I want it to be a story of responsibility.
If I got the chance to learn despite the circumstances, I want to use that education in service of others.
And if there are institutional obstacles facing graduates, I want to be part of the solution that helps overcome them.
message: We are not asking to remain prisoners of the past.
And we don't want to use the past against the state.
We want to take the lessons of the past and use them to build better institutions for the future.
We want education to be a bridge between Syrians and their state, between the certificate and the opportunity, between the past and the future.
The Syrian people have suffered enough; the next stage must be one of building and empowering the person.
excerpt: We are not asking to remain prisoners of the past.

title: From an Interior-Design Engineering Classroom to the Fields of Humanitarian Work — When Determination Becomes Stronger Than War
paragraphs: My academic journey began with studying interior-design engineering, and I had a clear dream of building my future in the field I loved. But the war changed so much about my life, as it did for thousands of young Syrians.
In 2021 I stopped attending university — not for lack of will or ambition, but because of the circumstances the years of war and instability imposed.
I left Damascus and returned to Deir ez-Zor in search of a new beginning, and in a place where the road was anything but easy, I tried to find myself another chance.
I refused to accept that circumstances would be the end of my education.
I enrolled at the University of the People to study a business administration diploma, and at the same time began searching for work opportunities that would let me support myself and my family.
I was studying and working at the same time — carrying the weight of the present while constantly thinking about the future.

Over the following years, I worked with several humanitarian organizations in north and east Syria, moving through various administrative roles and gaining experience in monitoring and evaluation, data collection, field work, and accountability and coordination.
Those jobs were never just a source of income — they were a real school that taught me the meaning of responsibility and working for the community.
Today, I'm proud that I never let circumstances define my ending.

I started as a student in an engineering major, was forced to stop, then returned to education by a different path, worked alongside my studies, and built professional experience in the humanitarian field.
But a graduate's journey doesn't end the day they receive their certificate.
A graduate needs a clear path to make use of their qualification in further study, in work, and in contributing to building their country.
message: Cities may change, studies may stop, opportunities may be delayed — but a person can always start again.
We are a generation that learned the road may not be straight, but that doesn't mean it has no end.
Education gave me a new chance, work gave me experience, and determination kept me moving forward.
excerpt: Cities may change, studies may stop, opportunities may be delayed — but a person can always start again.

title: When University Stumbled… the Dream Didn't
paragraphs: I had one clear wish: to finish my education and earn a degree that would help me build an independent future.
But the circumstances Syria went through made university education far harder for me. My plan was derailed more than once, and I had to keep rethinking the path I could take.
For a long time, I felt the years of my life were passing while my dream stood still.
Then I discovered distance university education.
The decision wasn't easy. I had to learn how to study differently, organize my time, and balance my daily responsibilities with my studies.
I would open lectures at home, study in whatever hours I could carve out of my day, and try not to let exhaustion make me give up.
Over time, studying became a fixed part of my life.
The certificate was never just a piece of paper to me.
It was proof to myself that, despite everything that happened, I was still capable of reaching the goal I had set for myself.
When I finally graduated, I felt I had closed a long chapter of waiting.
But then a new question appeared:
How can I make use of this qualification in my own country?

A graduate doesn't just need access to education — they also need a clear path after graduation, one that lets them use their knowledge and experience in work, continued study, and serving their community.
message: Circumstances may take years from us, but they must not take our future.
Every Syrian graduate carries, behind their certificate, a story of patience and struggle.
What we need today is for these certificates and experiences to be turned into energy that Syrian society can benefit from.
excerpt: Circumstances may take years from us, but they must not take our future.

title: A Certificate Years in the Waiting… and a Future Waiting for Its Recognition
paragraphs: My educational journey wasn't easy.

I dreamed of earning a university degree and using it to build a stable career, but the educational, economic, and security circumstances we went through made the road far more complicated than I had expected.
As the years passed, it became clear to me that the traditional path wasn't the only path.
So I turned to distance education and began a new chapter of my life.
I worked while I studied, trying to cover my daily needs while still keeping up with university requirements.
There were days I felt exhausted, and others when the road felt endless, but one thought kept me going:
I don't want the years of my youth to pass without giving myself a real chance.
I kept studying until I graduated.
I thought the hardest stage was behind me.
But I discovered that earning the certificate might be the beginning of another challenge.
When a graduate wants to continue their studies or look for work that relies on their qualification, recognition of that qualification becomes a fundamental issue.
That's when I felt I wasn't alone.
There are many Syrian graduates holding degrees from different universities, facing similar questions about how their qualifications can be recognized and put to use.
message: We don't want our certificates to stay hanging on the wall.
We want to use them.
We want to finish our education, work, and contribute to our society.
Real investment in Syria begins with the person who kept learning despite every circumstance.
excerpt: We don't want our certificates to stay hanging on the wall.

title: I Wasn't Looking for an Easy Path… I Was Only Looking for a Possible One
paragraphs: I used to think earning a university degree was the hardest part of the journey.
But I discovered that reaching university under difficult circumstances requires a different kind of determination.
I didn't have all the tools a student usually needs. I had to study from home and deal with power outages, weak internet, and a lack of time.
Some days I would start studying knowing the connection could drop at any moment.
Other days I would put off my own personal needs just to make time to study.
Distance education was never a luxury for me.
It was a window.
A window that made me feel my future was still open, even as the options around me kept narrowing.
The years passed, and I learned a great deal — not only in my field, but in managing time, discipline, and taking on responsibility.
Then I reached graduation.
It was a moment I had waited a long time for.
But the joy of graduating came with an important question: what now?
How can a graduate move from education into work?
How can they find out the status of their qualification?
And how can they get a fair chance to benefit from the years of study they put in?
message: I want every student beginning their educational journey today to have a clear path after graduation.
It's not enough to open the doors of education to people.
We must also help them open the doors to the future.
excerpt: I want every student beginning their educational journey today to have a clear path after graduation.

title: From Working to Support the Family to Building a Professional Future
paragraphs: I never had the luxury of being just a student.
From an early age, I had to work and carry part of my family's responsibilities.
That's why the decision to return to education was such a major challenge.

I knew studying would take time and effort, but I also knew that not studying meant I might stay for years in a cycle of work without ever gaining the qualification that would help me develop my career.
I chose distance education.
I studied after finishing work, sometimes late into the night.
There was no lecture hall waiting for me, no daily commute to a campus.
I had a device, an internet connection, books and lectures, and the will to keep going.
Little by little, I began to feel that the years I feared would be wasted were turning into experience and knowledge.
I reached graduation.
But I realized that graduating wasn't the end.
There's an entire generation of Syrian graduates who need to move from proving they can learn to proving they can work and contribute.
message: We aren't asking to be given opportunities we haven't earned.
We're asking for a clear, fair mechanism that lets us prove what we've learned and put it to use.
We learned despite the war, and today we want to contribute to building what comes after it.
excerpt: We aren't asking to be given opportunities we haven't earned.

title: A Mother, a Student, and a Graduate… Three Battles in a Single Day
paragraphs: Studying was never a journey separate from the rest of my life.
I was a mother with family responsibilities, and at the same time I wanted to return to education after years in which I felt circumstances had taken so many opportunities from me.
When I began studying remotely, I didn't know if I'd be able to keep going.
I had to find time to study amid my daily responsibilities.
Sometimes I studied in the morning, sometimes at night, and sometimes I made use of a few spare minutes between one responsibility and another.
The path wasn't ideal, but it was possible.
And with every subject I finished, I felt I was reclaiming part of a dream I thought I had lost.
Until I reached graduation day.
In that moment, I wasn't only thinking about the certificate.
I thought about every day I nearly gave up, and every time I told myself I would keep going.
Today, I hope the path after graduation becomes clearer — for me, and for other Syrian graduates.
message: Education doesn't only change the life of the student.
Sometimes it changes the life of an entire family.
And when a person gets a real chance to learn, they don't just build their own future — they become able to be part of their community's future too.
excerpt: Education doesn't only change the life of the student.

title: When Place Was No Longer an Excuse to Stop
paragraphs: I used to believe that my surrounding circumstances determined what I could achieve.
But over time I realized I might not be able to change every circumstance — but I could decide not to let them stop me.
I chose distance education because access to traditional education wasn't available to me the way I needed it.
I started almost from zero.
I learned how to organize my time, how to study independently, and how to seek out information instead of waiting for it to come to me.
The experience was hard, but it made me more self-reliant.
Over time, studying turned from an attempt to escape reality into a way of building a different future.
I reached graduation, but I discovered another challenge waiting for me: how do I make use of my qualification?
A graduate needs more than a certificate.
They need recognition of their education, a chance to work, the possibility of continuing their studies, and an institution to turn to when they face an obstacle they can't solve alone.
message: If education gave us a chance to start again, then we have the right to find a clear path to use what we've learned.
We don't want to be a lost generation after graduation; we want to be a generation that takes part in building Syria.
excerpt: If education gave us a chance to start again, then we have the right to find a clear path to use what we've learned.
